reasoning: The failure-driven edits take priority and add focused guidance outside the protected section: one on comparing logical scope and conclusion types, and one on validating reductions and imported estimates. The success-driven edits address distinct checks not covered by those failure edits, so I preserve all four. No edits target content within the protected markers.

edits.content:
### Compare logical scope and conclusion type
Treat stronger-choice questions as partial-order comparisons: existence or smoothness alone does not establish a rate, sign, uniqueness up to scaling, or structural localization. A restriction on parameters that occur does not assert that every permitted parameter occurs; decidability does not imply witness construction; and plain isomorphism does not imply preservation of a specified map or action. Likewise, an upper bound does not supply a matching lower bound. For equivalence questions, distinguish the exact principle from nearby alternatives. Compare direction, scope, structural data, term-to-parameter placement, coefficients, and index ranges; do not add exceptional cases without evidence.

### Validate reductions and imported estimates
Before reducing a named quantity or event to an easier representation, pin down its convention and the exact event or solution class, and establish equivalence under the stated hypotheses. Preserve the theorem’s normalization, including unit constants, and check its hypotheses and data spaces before importing a regularity result. Do not add quantitative bounds or dependencies unless they follow from the stated result. When structural conditions appear equivalent, translate each into the relevant invariant and test boundary cases before identifying them.

For parameterized runtime claims, distinguish FPT bounds of the form f(k)n^c, where c is independent of k, from XP bounds of the form n^{g(k)}. Polynomial time for each fixed k alone does not establish FPT; check whether the input-size exponent depends on the parameter.

For a strict log-concavity claim, check the strict inequality at every claimed index: a flat triple gives equality, and plateau boundaries require their own check. Trapezoidality or unimodality alone does not imply strict log-concavity.

For a complete classification, keep probability modalities and eventual-event conditions separate. Almost-sure convergence to one of several limits does not mean each limit occurs almost surely; positive probability of a branch does not imply certainty or automatic absorption. Match the claimed outcomes and events to the option exactly.

When comparing quantifiers, write their order explicitly, especially whether a witness may be chosen separately for each target or must work for all targets. Preserve the order of nested limits and distinguish limit superior from limit inferior: a limsup of −∞ forces eventual divergence to −∞, whereas a liminf of −∞ may hold only along a subsequence. Do not assume a liminf growth-exponent bound implies a constant-factor counting bound at the endpoint exponent; verify that implication.
